newsitem.title: UK: U.S. faces trouble abroad, but seen pushing hard.
newsitem.headline: U.S. faces trouble abroad, but seen pushing hard.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

U.S. President Bill Clinton faces a world of troubles in his second term, from the Middle East to China, and is expected to keep pushing an aggressive foreign policy that has recently upset some allies and partners.

Diplomats say the Clinton administration, after a shaky start on foreign policy, has shown increasing confidence that peaked with Washington's role in brokering the Bosnian peace agreement one year ago.
European and Asian countries see Clinton's win in the U.S. elections as a welcome sign of continuity that will carry the world's only remaining superpower into the 21st century.
Nevertheless, Washington has upset some of its closest allies this year on issues ranging from trade to terrorism.

"The Americans have been willing to push ahead with their own interests in a very aggressive way and I don't see that changing," said one European diplomat. "Clinton is more secure now and he'll really want to make his mark."
Professor Sir Laurence Martin, director of the Royal Institute of International Affairs (RIIA) in London, agreed.
"We could get a slightly more aggressive policy, particularly on trade and perhaps in the Middle East," he said.

Diplomats say this could be reflected in an expected reshuffle among U.S. policymakers. Secretary of State Warren Christopher is expected to retire and may be replaced by Madeleine Albright, currently U.S. envoy to the United Nations.

Albright has a more aggressive, although less intellectual reputation than the mild-mannered Christopher. Washington insiders say Richard Holbrooke, the hard-hitting architect of the Bosnian peace deal, may take over at the United Nations.
One of the first decisions for Clinton now will be on whether to extend the crucial U.S. contribution to the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia beyond the end of this year.
That decision, potentially unpopular in the United States, could not be taken before he had secured a second term. Washington is widely expected to keep some troops in Bosnia.
It may prove to be one of the easier problems to solve.
Clinton will be hampered by major cutbacks in the funding of U.S. diplomacy over the last few years and by the fact that the opposition Republicans still control Congress.
The Middle East peace process is in turmoil but the U.S. administration is expected to try hard in breaking the logjam.
"Clinton will keep this as one of his top priorities but I can't see much hope of progress any time soon," said Maha Azzam of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
Iran and Iraq are still defying the United States, with clear differences between Washington and European allies over how best to deal with Iran in particular.

China's future as the new power in Asia is unclear and relations with Washington have been strained over human rights, trade and military tensions with Taiwan. Ties with China and the rest of Asia will be near the top of the U.S. agenda.

In Europe, pushing through NATO enlargement without alienating an insecure Russia will be difficult. A NATO summit next May or June is expected to make decisions on which Eastern European countries will be able to join the alliance.

Clinton's good working relationship with Russian President Boris Yeltsin may help overcome many hurdles in an often testy relationship with Moscow. But no one knows how long Yeltsin, who underwent heart bypass surgery on Tuesday, will last.

Washington is locked in disputes with the 15-nation European Union on a range of trade issues and has also shown irritation with EU attempts to build a bigger role for itself in foreign policy, including in the Middle East.
"The basic reality hasn't changed. We have aspirations but they do not match the power of the Americans," said another European diplomat. "It will continue to be a problem."

The United Nations, suffering from an identity crisis and deeply in debt, is looking for a new secretary-general after Washington angered its partners by publicly vetoing a second term for Boutros Boutros-Ghali and demanding more U.N. reforms.
Washington has been embarrassed by constant reminders from its allies that it owes most of the debt that has driven the United Nations close to bankruptcy. Solutions must be found.

Arms control, so often led by the United States, has also run into trouble recently. A nuclear test ban treaty completed in September may never come into effect, the U.S. Senate has not yet ratified a global pact banning chemical weapons and there is a row with Moscow on missile defences and nuclear arms deals.
One crisis which is unlikely to draw much U.S. involvement is the current humanitarian disaster in Zaire, despite French appeals for an international force to be sent to the region.
"U.S. interest in most of sub-Saharan Africa is minimal," said Michael Cox, an analyst of U.S. foreign policy.
"The Americans have too many other things of strategic interest to worry about."
